analysis.one_liner: Forces the EPA to classify toxic "forever chemicals" as hazardous and helps water systems treat them.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 241-183, with 23 Republicans joining all voting Democrats, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS ("forever chemicals") are man-made substances used in nonstick cookware, water-resistant clothing, firefighting foam, and many industrial processes that do not break down in the environment and may cause serious health problems. This bill would order the EPA to designate the two best-known ones, PFOA and PFOS, as hazardous substances under the Superfund law, requiring cleanup of contaminated sites. It would also force the EPA to set national drinking water standards for PFAS, limit industrial discharges into rivers and streams, test all PFAS for toxicity, regulate how PFAS waste is incinerated, and hand out grants so small towns and schools can test and filter their water.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of people who drink contaminated water, especially in communities near PFAS manufacturing plants, military bases, and airports where firefighting foam was used. The bill prioritizes grant money for disadvantaged communities, funds testing and filtration in schools, and creates a public website so households on private wells can get their water tested. People exposed through the air or workplace also benefit from hazardous-air-pollutant listing and regulated waste disposal.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to designate PFOA and PFOS as hazardous substances under the Superfund law within one year, triggering cleanup of contaminated sites, and to decide within five years whether all other PFAS belong on the list.

Requires a national drinking water regulation for PFAS, including standards for PFOA and PFOS, within two years, and authorizes up to $500 million a year through 2026 in grants to help community water systems pay for treatment technology, with priority for disadvantaged communities.

Sets deadlines for the EPA to publish Clean Water Act health criteria for PFAS and to set discharge limits for nine major polluting industries, including pulp and paper, textiles, metal finishing, and plastics.
Funds $100 million a year in school drinking water testing and filtration grants, creates a household well-water testing website, and requires guidance to reduce firefighters' exposure to PFAS foam.

Requires toxicity testing of all PFAS, bans unsafe incineration of PFAS waste, and requires PFAS manufacturers to turn over analytical reference standards so states and the EPA can detect and enforce against contamination.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical companies that make PFAS and the nine listed industries that discharge them, which would face cleanup liability, discharge limits, mandatory toxicity testing, and new reporting duties. Airports would carry some remaining cleanup exposure for their non-foam releases. Water utilities and their ratepayers would face compliance costs, softened by federal grants.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars the EPA from imposing any financial penalties for violating the new PFAS drinking water standard for five years after the rule is issued, giving water systems and industrial users a long grace period.
It gives airport sponsors a full Superfund liability shield for PFAS releases from federally required firefighting foam, shifting those cleanup costs to the public and other responsible parties.
Cleanup liability and discharge limits raise costs for manufacturers, which may be passed to consumers in the prices of products like cookware, clothing, and carpet.

A good-faith objection: the bill mandates many EPA actions on fixed deadlines covering thousands of PFAS compounds, and some of the standards could be difficult to set on sound science in the required timeframes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: enforceable drinking water limits, mandated cleanup of contaminated sites, discharge limits for major polluters, and direct federal money so small towns and schools do not have to absorb treatment costs alone. The real costs fall on the industries that created and profit from PFAS, though some of those costs would reach consumers through prices and ratepayers through utility bills. The bill's own soft spots are real: a five-year penalty moratorium on the drinking water rule and a liability carve-out for airports dilute the enforcement it promises. On balance the gains to public health outweigh those concessions, which is why the bill cleared the House with bipartisan votes at every stage.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in July 2021, but the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never acted on it, so the bill died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2021 by Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan with 49 cosponsors, 44 Democrats and 5 Republicans.
It advanced through the House Energy and Commerce Committee with bipartisan votes at each stage: 16-7 at subcommittee in June and 33-20 when the full committee ordered it reported in July 2021.

On July 21, 2021, House Republicans offered a motion to recommit the bill to committee, a last chance to stop it, which failed 204-218, with every voting Democrat opposed and every voting Republican in favor.
The House then passed the bill 241-183, with 218 Democrats and 23 Republicans in favor.
The Senate received the bill on July 22, 2021 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which took no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The PFAS provisions that did become law in this period came through other vehicles, such as the infrastructure law, not this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and the industrial dischargers listed in the bill are better off, because they avoided Superfund cleanup liability, mandatory discharge limits, and toxicity testing requirements. Communities with contaminated drinking water got nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS makers and dischargers avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was 241-183 with 23 of 211 Republicans joining all 218 voting Democrats, and the bill also cleared committee on bipartisan votes, but the Senate, controlled by Democrats, simply never took it up.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers (3M, DuPont, Chemours and similar chemical makers)
industries.note: The bill would designate their flagship products as Superfund hazardous substances, require toxicity testing of every PFAS they make, force turnover of analytical standards for enforcement, and deem new PFAS an unreasonable risk pending EPA review. Their interest in defeating the bill ran directly against the public's interest in cleanup and safe drinking water.

industries.industry: Industrial dischargers (pulp and paper, textiles, electroplating, metal finishing, leather tanning, paints, electronics, plastics)
industries.note: The bill names nine priority industries that would face mandatory PFAS discharge limits into public waters and must notify treatment plants before introducing PFAS. Their discharge is the contamination the public drinks.

The bill gives airport sponsors a Superfund liability shield for PFAS releases from federally required firefighting foam, protecting them from cleanup costs the public would otherwise recover from them. The airports' gain comes at the expense of whoever else pays for the cleanup.

industries.industry: Public water systems and publicly owned treatment works
industries.note: They face new monitoring, treatment, and discharge obligations, but the bill offsets the cost with up to $500 million a year in treatment grants plus $200 million a year for treatment works, and bars penalties for five years after the drinking water rule.

industries.industry: Water treatment and testing technology firms
industries.note: Grant-funded installation of filtration systems, mandatory testing in schools, and a published EPA list of approved treatment technologies create demand for their products, alongside the public's interest in clean water.
